User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $650 in work sup

plies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Nice — you’ve given the key pieces. Below I’ll summarize what’s deductible, whether you should itemize, how to handle the home office for your consulting work, and which federal (and a note about Oregon) forms/worksheets you’ll use. I’ll also show quick back‑of‑the‑envelope numbers so you can see the tax impact.

Quick facts you gave (2023)
- Filing status: Married filing jointly, live in Por

tland, OR
- W-2 wages: $84,900
- Self‑employment (consulting) income: $22,100
- Interest: $920 (Marcus savings)
- Dividends: $195 (Fidelity)
- Home office: 165 sq ft out of 690 sq ft (165/690 = 23.91% ≈ 24%)
- Rent: $2,050/month → $24,600/year
- Student loan interest paid: $2,700
- Charitable cash gift: $800 (have receipt)
- Work supplies: $650

What’s deductible (federal)
- Consulting business (self‑employment) expenses — deductible on Schedule C:
  - Work supplies: $650 (ordinary & necessary business expe

nse).
  - Home office: allowed for your consulting if you meet “regular and exclusive” business‑use rules. You can use either the simplified method or the regular method (details below).
  - Any other ordinary business expenses you have (phone portion, business mileage, etc.) are also deductible on Schedule C.
- Self‑employment tax: you pay SE tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net self‑employment income and you can deduct one‑half of the SE tax as an adjustment to income on Form 1040.
- Student loan inter

est: up to $2,500 (adjustment to income) if your MAGI is below the phaseout range. For MFJ in 2023 the phaseout begins at $145,000 and is complete at $175,000. Based on the numbers you gave (about $100k AGI before this deduction), you should be eligible for the full $2,500 (you paid $2,700, so deductible amount is $2,500).
- Charitable gift ($800): deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). Not deductible above the line.

What is NOT deductible (for most W-2 employees)
- If any portion of your home office

time were for your W-2 employer (and you are not a statutory employee), unreimbursed employee home office expenses are NOT deductible (suspended through 2025). However, because you have self‑employment consulting income, the home office deduction can apply to the consulting business portion (Schedule C).

Home office: regular vs simplified method (and quick numbers)
- Office % = 165 / 690 ≈ 23.91% → round to 24%.
- Rent = $24,600/year

Regular method
- Deduct business share of actual home expenses (rent, u

tilities, renter’s insurance, etc.) multiplied by business percentage. With just rent given:
  - Home office deduction (rent portion) ≈ 24% × $24,600 = $5,904.
  - If you have utilities or renter’s insurance, add those pro‑rata shares too.
- You report home office expenses on Form 8829 (Business Use of Your Home) and attach it to Schedule C. The deduction reduces your Schedule C net profit.

Simplified method
- $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 165 sq ft × $5 = $825.
- No Form 8829 necessary; you claim the sim

plified amount on Schedule C.

Which method is better here?
- Based solely on rent, the regular method (≈ $5,904) gives a much larger deduction than simplified ($825). So regular method likely better — unless you expect limits, special circumstances, or prefer simplified recordkeeping. Note: home office deduction cannot exceed your gross income from that business minus other business expenses — but with $22,100 consulting and only $650 supplies, $5,904 should be allowable.

Rough tax-impact calculation (ill

ustrative)
- Schedule C gross: $22,100
- Less supplies: -$650
- Less home office (regular): -$5,904
- Net profit ≈ $15,546
- Self‑employment tax: SE taxable = 92.35% × 15,546 ≈ 14,362 → SE tax ≈ 14,362 × 15.3% ≈ $2,196
- Deductible half of SE tax (above the line): ≈ $1,098
- Student loan interest deduction: $2,500 (max)
- Charitable deduction only helps if you itemize.

Standard vs itemize?
- 2023 standard deduction for MFJ = $27,700.
- Your only known itemizable amounts: charitable $800 and any state & loc

al taxes (SALT) paid (state income tax or property tax). You didn’t list SALT amounts. Unless your state tax + other itemizable items (medical, mortgage interest, property tax, etc.) exceed about $27k, standard deduction will be larger.
- Important: the home office deduction and business expenses reduce your Schedule C net profit and therefore reduce AGI whether you take the standard deduction or itemize. So those business deductions help you either way.
- Conclusion (based on info given): you will most lik

ely take the standard deduction, because $800 charity by itself is far below the standard deduction. If you want a firm answer, tell me your 2023 state income tax withheld (from W‑2 Box 17) and any property tax or mortgage interest — I can recompute.

Forms & worksheets you’ll use (Federal)
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report the $22,100 consulting income and business expenses (supplies, home office-related items, etc.). If you received 1099‑NEC(s), include those

amounts.
- Form 8829 (if you use the regular method for home office) — for business use of home. (If you use the simplified method, you don’t use 8829.)
- Schedule SE — to compute self‑employment tax.
- 1040 Schedule 1 (Part II adjustments) — half of SE tax and student loan interest deduction flow here (these are above‑the‑line adjustments).
- Schedule A — only if you choose to itemize (for charitable deductions and SALT up to $10,000).
- Keep Form 1098‑E (student loan interest statement) as proof for the $

2,500 deduction.
- Keep receipts for the $800 charitable gift (it’s required for cash gifts $250+ to substantiate).
- State return: Oregon (OR-40 and any applicable schedules). Oregon generally starts from federal AGI with state modifications; consult Oregon instructions or a preparer for state-specific adjustments (but the Schedule C deductions and SE adjustments typically flow through). Make sure to include any Oregon-specific credits or rules.

Other practical notes / recommendations
- Be sure you receiv

ed/can find any 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC for the consulting. Even if you didn’t receive a 1099, you must report the income.
- Keep documentation: receipts for supplies, rent/lease statements, evidence of square footage and exclusive use, mileage logs (if you deduct vehicle expenses), 1098‑E, and charity receipts.
- Consider retirement contributions for your consulting income (SEP‑IRA or Solo 401(k)) — these could reduce taxable income further and lower SE tax exposure.
- Because you have self‑employment income

, you may owe additional tax beyond what was withheld from your W‑2 (SE tax plus any income tax on the consulting profit). If you expect similar income next year, consider quarterly estimated tax payments to avoid penalties.
- If you want, I can run a more detailed estimated tax calculation (taxable income, income tax plus SE tax, estimated refund/amount due) — I’d need W‑2 federal withholding, any state tax withheld, and whether you have other adjustments or deductions.

Limitations / disclaimer
- This is

general guidance based on the facts you provided. For personalized tax planning or filing help (particularly state-specific issues or complex items), consider consulting a CPA or tax preparer.

Next steps I can help with
- Recalculate with the regular vs simplified home office using any utilities/renter’s insurance you paid.
- Compute estimated federal tax and self‑employment tax and show whether you’ll owe or get a refund (I’ll need W‑2 tax withholding and any estimated payments).
- Draft a checklist of re

cords to assemble for your preparer or for DIY filing.

Would you like me to:
1) compute a more precise estimate of your 2023 federal tax (need W‑2 federal withheld and any state withholding), or
2) calculate exact home‑office numbers using any utility/insurance amounts you paid in 2023?
